pros: Cascade agent edits across files, runs commands and reads the output
Cheaper Pro plan than Cursor with a usable free credit allowance
Previews let you click a rendered element and send it as context
Switch between several providers' models plus cheaper in-house models per request
Hybrid enterprise deployment keeps indexing and inference in your own cloud
cons: Credit multipliers per model make the monthly allowance hard to predict
JetBrains and Neovim plugins get completions and chat, not full Cascade
Ownership and pricing changed repeatedly in 2025
verdict_line: Pick Windsurf if you want a Cursor-style agentic editor at a lower monthly price and can tolerate a credit-based allowance.

pros: GPU-rendered Rust editor opens large repos and files without stutter
Bring your own API keys or a local model at no extra charge
Agent panel shows every change as a per-hunk reviewable diff
External agents like Claude Code run inside the editor via ACP
Built-in pair programming with shared cursors and voice
cons: Extension ecosystem is far smaller than VS Code's
Windows build arrived later and lags macOS and Linux on polish
No SSO, admin controls or usage reporting for enterprise rollouts
Edit prediction is weaker than Cursor's tab completion
verdict_line: Pick Zed if editor speed matters most and you want AI through your own API keys or local models rather than a vendor credit plan.

pros: Runs long multi-step tasks in the terminal, rerunning tests until they pass
Works with any editor and unattended in CI, not only inside an IDE
Hooks and permission rules control what it may run without approval
Project conventions live in versioned markdown files in the repo
Responds to mentions on GitHub issues and pull requests
cons: No free plan; evaluation needs a paid subscription or API credits
Anthropic models only, so no cross-provider comparison per task
Not an inline completion tool, so most teams pair it with one
Metered API use gets expensive on long agent sessions
verdict_line: Pick Claude Code if you want an agent you can delegate whole tasks to from the terminal, your IDE and CI rather than an autocomplete.

pros: Chat inside the AWS console reads your actual resources and IAM policies
Slash-command agents generate tests and review code in the IDE
Java upgrade transformation agent handles large legacy migrations
Free tier works with a Builder ID, no AWS account required
Pro seats provisioned through IAM Identity Center land on the AWS bill
cons: General coding quality trails Cursor and Copilot outside AWS work
No choice of models; you use what AWS provides
Overlap with AWS's separate Kiro editor confuses the roadmap
Builder ID versus Identity Center sign-in trips up new users
verdict_line: Pick Amazon Q Developer if most of your work is on AWS and you want an assistant that understands your account, services and IAM setup.

pros: Runs on-premises, in your VPC or fully air-gapped
Provenance flags suggestions that match public code and shows the licence
Switch between Tabnine's protected model and third-party models per team
First-class JetBrains plugin alongside VS Code, Visual Studio and Eclipse
Admin console reports usage by user and model
cons: Task-specific agents, no iterative multi-file agent like Cursor or Claude Code
In-house model completions are weaker than frontier providers
No free plan, so casual evaluation is harder
Positioning has shifted several times, from autocomplete to privacy to agents
verdict_line: Pick Tabnine if your security policy requires an AI assistant that runs on-premises or air-gapped with licence provenance on suggestions.
